thrombolysis.name: NINDS
thrombolysis.question: Does IV alteplase within 3h of symptom onset improve outcomes in acute ischemic stroke?
thrombolysis.design: RCT, n=624, alteplase 0.9 mg/kg vs placebo within 3h
thrombolysis.outcomes: Study 2 (333 participants): mRS 0-1 at 3 months, 38.7% versus 26.1%. Across both studies (624 participants), symptomatic ICH within 36 hours occurred in 6.4% versus 0.6%.
thrombolysis.nnt: Study 2: approximately 8 treated for one additional mRS 0-1 outcome at 3 months.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: IV alteplase within 3h improves neurologic recovery despite bleeding risk. Foundation of modern stroke treatment.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: Earlier treatment produced greater benefit in the alteplase individual-patient meta-analysis (Emberson 2014): approximately 10 percentage points of disability-free survival gained within 3 hours versus 5 at 3-4.5 hours. AHA Target: Stroke Elite Plus benchmarks include door-to-needle within 45 minutes for at least 75%, and within 30 minutes for at least 50%, of eligible patients.

thrombolysis.name: ECASS III
thrombolysis.question: Is IV alteplase effective 3-4.5h after symptom onset?
thrombolysis.design: RCT, n=821, alteplase vs placebo in 3-4.5h window
thrombolysis.bottomLine: Alteplase improved 90-day outcome in the selected 3-4.5-hour trial population. Cross-trial NNT and bleeding comparisons require matching endpoints, definitions and populations.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: The trial excluded age over 80, NIHSS over 25, combined prior stroke and diabetes, and oral anticoagulant use. These historical enrollment restrictions are not a complete current treatment-eligibility checklist; use the current AHA/ASA guidance and prescribing information.

thrombolysis.name: EXTEND-IA TNK
thrombolysis.question: Is TNK non-inferior to alteplase before EVT for LVO?
thrombolysis.design: RCT, n=202, TNK 0.25 mg/kg vs alteplase 0.9 mg/kg before EVT
thrombolysis.outcomes: Substantial reperfusion: 22% vs 10% (P=0.002 for noninferiority; P=0.03 for superiority). mRS 0-2 at 90d: 64% vs 51%.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: TNK superior to alteplase for early reperfusion in LVO.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: TNK is non-inferior to alteplase for AIS and may be superior for LVO. Single bolus (vs 1-hr infusion) → logistic advantage for drip-and-ship.

thrombolysis.name: AcT
thrombolysis.question: Is tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg noninferior to alteplase 0.9 mg/kg in adults with disabling AIS who are otherwise eligible for IV thrombolysis?
thrombolysis.design: Canadian multicenter RCT within 4.5 hours: 1600 randomized; 1577 included in the intention-to-treat analysis (806 tenecteplase, 771 alteplase).
thrombolysis.outcomes: mRS 0-1 at 90-120d: 36.9% (TNK) vs 34.8% (alteplase), meeting non-inferiority. sICH: 3.4% vs 3.2%.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: TNK is non-inferior to alteplase in real-world AIS. Simpler single-bolus administration.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: The trial supports tenecteplase as an alternative to alteplase within its disabling-stroke eligibility criteria. Its single-bolus administration differs from the alteplase bolus-plus-infusion regimen; this trial did not measure institutional adoption.

thrombolysis.name: WAKE-UP
thrombolysis.question: Does alteplase benefit patients with unknown-onset stroke if DWI-FLAIR mismatch is present?
thrombolysis.design: RCT, n=503: alteplase versus placebo for unknown-onset stroke selected by DWI-FLAIR mismatch; patients with planned thrombectomy were excluded. Mismatch estimates lesion age but does not establish the true onset time.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: DWI-FLAIR mismatch identifies wake-up stroke patients within "tissue window" for lysis.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: MRI mismatch can select some unknown-onset patients for alteplase within the studied clinical and symptom-recognition window. Imaging does not remove the remaining treatment-time and eligibility requirements.

thrombolysis.name: EXTEND
thrombolysis.question: Does alteplase benefit patients 4.5-9h from onset with CTP/MRP mismatch?
thrombolysis.design: RCT, n=225: alteplase versus placebo with perfusion mismatch, core <70 mL, mismatch ratio >1.2 and absolute mismatch >10 mL.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: Perfusion mismatch extends lytic window to 9h in selected patients.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: The historical EXTEND profile used core <70 mL, mismatch ratio >1.2 and absolute mismatch >10 mL. Extended-window selection remains specific to treatment, timing, imaging and the remaining eligibility criteria.

thrombolysis.name: TIMELESS
thrombolysis.question: Does tenecteplase at 4.5-24 hours improve outcomes in perfusion-selected LVO stroke, in a trial where most participants underwent thrombectomy?
thrombolysis.design: RCT, n=458: tenecteplase versus placebo 4.5-24 hours after last known well; 77.3% underwent thrombectomy.
thrombolysis.outcomes: Primary ordinal mRS at 90d: adjusted common OR 1.13 (95% CI 0.82-1.57, P=0.45) — neutral; median mRS 3 in both groups. 77.3% underwent thrombectomy. Mortality 19.7% vs 18.2%; sICH 3.2% vs 2.3%.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: No incremental functional benefit was demonstrated in this population. No statistically significant safety difference was detected; the trial does not establish safety equivalence.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: The neutral superiority result does not prove that EVT alone is noninferior for every late-window patient. Interpret TIMELESS in its perfusion-selected population and substantial thrombectomy use.

thrombolysis.name: TRACE-2
thrombolysis.question: Is TNK non-inferior to alteplase in Chinese AIS patients ineligible for EVT?
thrombolysis.design: RCT, n=1430, TNK vs alteplase ≤4.5h, Chinese population
thrombolysis.bottomLine: TNK non-inferior to alteplase in EVT-ineligible AIS (NIHSS 5-25). Confirms AcT findings in different population.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: TRACE-2 + AcT establish TNK as standard-of-care alternative to alteplase across populations.

thrombolysis.name: TWIST
thrombolysis.question: Does TNK benefit wake-up stroke patients without advanced imaging selection?
thrombolysis.design: RCT, n=578, TNK vs standard care for wake-up stroke (no CTP/MRI required)
thrombolysis.outcomes: Primary ordinal mRS at 90d: adjusted OR 1.18 (95% CI 0.88-1.58, p=0.27) — no benefit. Mortality 10% vs 8%; sICH 2% vs 1%.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: Without advanced imaging selection, TNK did not improve outcomes in wake-up stroke.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: Noncontrast-CT selection in TWIST did not demonstrate a functional benefit from tenecteplase in wake-up stroke. The trial did not randomize imaging strategies or establish a universal requirement for advanced imaging in every late-window scenario.

thrombolysis.name: RAISE
thrombolysis.question: Is reteplase superior to alteplase within 4.5h of ischemic stroke?
thrombolysis.design: RCT, n=1412, China. Reteplase 18mg + 18mg boluses vs alteplase 0.9 mg/kg.
thrombolysis.outcomes: mRS 0-1 at 90d: 79.5% vs 70.4% (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.05-1.21; p=0.002 for superiority). sICH ≤36h 2.4% vs 2.0%. Any ICH at 90d HIGHER: 7.7% vs 4.9%.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: Reteplase beat alteplase for excellent outcome, but with more intracranial hemorrhage overall.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: Generalizability is limited by the China-only setting, exclusion of patients over 80 and EVT candidates, and underrepresentation of women. A guideline recommendation to consider a treatment is distinct from regulatory approval or a local protocol change.

thrombolysis.name: ARAMIS
thrombolysis.question: Can DAPT replace IV thrombolysis for minor NON-DISABLING stroke within 4.5h?
thrombolysis.design: Open-label non-inferiority RCT, n=760, 38 Chinese hospitals. NIHSS ≤5 with ≤1 point on key single items (median NIHSS 2). DAPT × 12 days vs alteplase.
thrombolysis.outcomes: mRS 0-1 at 90d: 93.8% (DAPT) vs 91.4% (alteplase); risk difference 2.3% (95% CI -1.5% to 6.2%); non-inferiority met (p<0.001). sICH 0.3% vs 0.9%.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: For genuinely non-disabling minor stroke, DAPT is a reasonable alternative to thrombolysis.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: Non-disabling status required clinical and patient assessment of usual activities and work, in addition to the NIHSS item limits. A low total NIHSS with a disabling deficit is not equivalent to this population; assess the actual disability.

thrombolysis.name: TASTE
thrombolysis.question: Is tenecteplase non-inferior to alteplase in patients selected by perfusion mismatch?
thrombolysis.design: Open-label non-inferiority RCT, n=680, 35 hospitals in 8 countries. TNK 0.25 mg/kg vs alteplase, perfusion target-mismatch required, EVT candidates excluded.
thrombolysis.outcomes: mRS 0-1 at 3mo: ITT 57% vs 55% (SRD 0.03, 95% CI -0.033 to 0.10) — non-inferiority NOT met in ITT; per-protocol 59% vs 56% — non-inferiority met. sICH 3% vs 2%.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: Supportive but not decisive: non-inferiority held per-protocol, not in intention-to-treat.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: The trial stopped early after other tenecteplase results emerged. For noninferiority, intention-to-treat analysis is not inherently conservative: nonadherence can make groups appear more similar. Interpret the prespecified intention-to-treat, per-protocol and sensitivity analyses together.

thrombolysis.name: TEMPO-2
thrombolysis.question: Does tenecteplase improve outcomes in minor stroke (NIHSS 0-5) with intracranial occlusion or a focal perfusion abnormality when there is clinical equipoise about thrombolysis?
thrombolysis.design: Open-label RCT with blinded outcomes, n=886, 48 hospitals in 10 countries. TNK 0.25 mg/kg vs non-thrombolytic standard care within 12h; intracranial occlusion or focal perfusion abnormality required. Stopped early for futility.
thrombolysis.outcomes: Return to premorbid baseline mRS at 90d: 72% vs 75% (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88-1.04, p=0.29). Death: 5% (20) vs 1% (5), adjusted HR 3.8 (95% CI 1.4-10.2, p=0.0085). sICH 2% vs <1%.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: Tenecteplase did not improve outcomes and showed possible harm in the enrolled minor-stroke population. This result is not a trial of every disabling or non-disabling low-NIHSS presentation.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: TEMPO-2 excluded patients for whom the physician and patient believed routine thrombolysis was warranted. Its clinical-equipoise population differs from ARAMIS; a vessel finding alone does not replace assessment of disability and eligibility.

thrombolysis.name: TRACE-III
thrombolysis.question: Does IV TNK at 4.5-24h benefit LVO patients WITHOUT access to thrombectomy?
thrombolysis.design: RCT, n=516, China. MCA/ICA occlusion with salvageable tissue on perfusion imaging and no EVT access. TNK 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) vs standard medical treatment; <2% received rescue EVT.
thrombolysis.bottomLine: Late-window TNK improves outcomes in perfusion-selected LVO when thrombectomy is not available.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: TRACE-III and TIMELESS studied different populations and patterns of EVT use. Their cross-trial contrast does not prove an interaction with EVT availability or establish tenecteplase as equivalent to thrombectomy. Do not use it to delay indicated EVT transfer.

thrombolysis.name: PROST / PROST-2
thrombolysis.citation: PROST JAMA Netw Open 2023;6:e2325415 (PMID 37490291); PROST-2 Lancet Neurol 2025;24:33-41 (PMID 39617030)
thrombolysis.question: Is IV recombinant human prourokinase non-inferior to alteplase within 4.5h?
thrombolysis.design: Two Chinese phase 3 open-label noninferiority RCTs. PROST excluded planned endovascular treatment; PROST-2 specifically enrolled patients ineligible for or refusing EVT. PROST-2: n=1552 at 61 hospitals; prourokinase 15 mg bolus plus 20 mg over 30 minutes versus alteplase 0.9 mg/kg.
thrombolysis.outcomes: PROST-2: mRS 0-1 at 90d 72.0% vs 68.7% (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.98-1.10; p<0.0001 for non-inferiority). sICH ≤36h LOWER: 0.3% vs 1.3% (p=0.021). PROST (2023) similarly met non-inferiority (mRS 0-1: 65.2% vs 64.3%).
thrombolysis.bottomLine: Prourokinase met noninferiority criteria in the selected trial populations. The significant symptomatic-ICH reduction was reported in PROST-2; PROST did not show a significant difference in that endpoint.
thrombolysis.teachingPoint: PROST concerns intravenous prourokinase, not PFO closure. Trial efficacy, indication-specific regulatory approval and local drug availability are separate questions.

thrombectomy.name: MR CLEAN
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT improve outcomes in acute anterior circulation LVO within 6h?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=500: intraarterial treatment plus usual care versus usual care; retrievable stents were used in 81.5% of the intervention group. Alteplase was given to 89% overall.
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS 0-2 at 90d: 33% vs 19%, aOR 2.16. sICH: 8% vs 6%.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: First unequivocally positive EVT trial, launching the modern thrombectomy era.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: The original five-trial HERMES individual-patient meta-analysis reported an NNT of 2.6 for one additional patient to improve by at least one mRS level at 90 days. This ordinal estimate is not an NNT for functional independence.

thrombectomy.name: ESCAPE
thrombectomy.question: Does rapid EVT with imaging selection benefit LVO within 12h?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=316: EVT versus usual care in patients with a small infarct core and moderate-to-good collateral circulation on CTA.
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS 0-2 at 90d: 53% vs 29%. NNT 4 for functional independence.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Collateral-based selection enables extended window.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: Good collaterals on CTA correlate with small core and viable penumbra — critical for late-window decisions.

thrombectomy.name: EXTEND-IA
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT benefit perfusion-selected LVO patients?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=70, CTP selection with core <70 mL, mismatch ratio >1.2, absolute mismatch >10 mL
thrombectomy.outcomes: Early neurologic improvement: 80% vs 37%. mRS 0-2 at 90d: 71% vs 40%.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: EVT improved outcomes in the perfusion-selected trial population. The study did not compare imaging-selection strategies or establish which strategy identifies the greatest benefit.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: EXTEND-IA validated perfusion-selected EVT. Its >1.2 / >10 mL mismatch profile later aligned with EXTEND IVT; DAWN used clinical-core mismatch, while DEFUSE-3 used stricter perfusion mismatch (ratio ≥1.8, mismatch ≥15 mL).

thrombectomy.name: SWIFT PRIME
thrombectomy.question: Does stent retriever EVT improve outcomes after IV tPA?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=196, tPA + EVT vs tPA alone
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Confirmed EVT benefit on top of IV tPA.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: Bridging thrombolysis + EVT was standard until trials questioned whether EVT alone might be non-inferior in patients presenting directly to thrombectomy-capable centres.

thrombectomy.name: DAWN
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT 6-24h from LKW benefit patients with clinical-core mismatch?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=206, tier-based inclusion (age, NIHSS, core volume)
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS 0-2 at 90d: 49% vs 13%. NNT 2.8 for functional independence.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Extended the EVT window to 24h with tissue-based selection.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: Historical DAWN mismatch tiers: age ≥80, NIHSS ≥10 and core <21 mL; age <80, NIHSS ≥10 and core <31 mL; or age <80, NIHSS ≥20 and core 31 to <51 mL. These are trial criteria, not the complete current EVT eligibility rules.

thrombectomy.name: DEFUSE-3
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT 6-16h benefit CTP-selected patients?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=182, core <70 mL + mismatch ratio ≥1.8 + mismatch volume ≥15 mL
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Perfusion-mismatch selection works up to 16h.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: DAWN and DEFUSE-3 provide historical trial-selection profiles. The January 2026 AHA/ASA guideline recommends 6-24-hour EVT for selected ICA/M1 LVO with NIHSS ≥6, prestroke mRS 0-1 and ASPECTS ≥6 (Class I, LOE A), with adjunctive perfusion imaging reasonable (Class IIa, LOE A). Apply the complete current recommendation rather than either trial profile alone.

thrombectomy.name: SELECT2
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT benefit patients with LARGE ischemic core (ASPECTS 3-5 or core ≥50 mL)?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=352, EVT vs medical management in 0-24h with large core
thrombectomy.bottomLine: EVT improved outcomes in selected patients with a large ischemic core. This does not establish benefit at every infarct volume, age, time window or degree of mass effect.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: Consider EVT in large-core patients with pre-stroke independence; counsel honestly about likelihood of moderate disability even with successful recanalization.

thrombectomy.name: ANGEL-ASPECT
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT benefit Chinese patients with ASPECTS 3-5?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=456, EVT vs medical management, within 24h of last known well
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Confirms SELECT2 in a different population.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: ANGEL-ASPECT, SELECT2 and RESCUE-Japan LIMIT support EVT for selected large-core stroke. Current eligibility also depends on vessel, time, age, NIHSS, prestroke function, imaging and mass effect; the results are not a blanket indication for every large infarct.

thrombectomy.name: RESCUE-Japan LIMIT
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT benefit patients with ASPECTS 3-5?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=203, Japanese population, 0-6h (or up to 24h if no early FLAIR change)
thrombectomy.outcomes: At 90 days, mRS 0-3 occurred in 31.0% versus 12.7% (approximate NNT 5.5). Symptomatic ICH: 9/100 (9.0%) versus 5/102 (4.9%); RR 1.84 (95% CI 0.64-5.29).
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Early large-core trial establishing EVT benefit in ASPECTS 3-5.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: The primary endpoint was mRS 0-3: moderate disability or better, including the ability to walk without assistance. It is broader than conventional functional independence (mRS 0-2); retain this distinction when discussing outcomes.

thrombectomy.name: BAOCHE + ATTENTION
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT benefit basilar artery occlusion?
thrombectomy.design: Two separate RCTs in Chinese populations
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS 0-3 at 90d: ATTENTION 46% vs 23% (aRR 2.06); BAOCHE 46% vs 24% (aRR 1.81). Mortality lower in ATTENTION (37% vs 55%, aRR 0.66); not significantly lower in BAOCHE (31% vs 42%, aRR 0.75, 95% CI 0.54-1.04).
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Basilar artery EVT improves outcomes in severely affected patients (NIHSS ≥10).
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: ATTENTION studied treatment within 12 hours with NIHSS ≥10; BAOCHE studied 6-24 hours and eventually allowed NIHSS ≥6. BASICS was neutral. Differences in enrollment and design may help interpretation but do not establish a single causal explanation for the contrasting results.

thrombectomy.name: MR CLEAN-LATE
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT help at 6-24h when patients are selected by CTA COLLATERALS rather than perfusion mismatch?
thrombectomy.design: RCT at 18 Dutch centers: 535 randomized, 502 included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. Anterior LVO at 6-24 hours with CTA collateral flow; patients already eligible under national DAWN/DEFUSE-3-based criteria were excluded.
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS shift at 90d: adjusted common OR 1.67 (95% CI 1.20-2.32); median mRS 3 vs 4. sICH HIGHER: 7% vs 2% (aOR 4.59, 95% CI 1.49-14.10). Mortality 24% vs 30% (NS).
thrombectomy.bottomLine: CTA-collateral-based selection supported EVT benefit in the trial’s selected 6-24-hour population outside the national perfusion-based eligibility pathway.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: Symptomatic ICH occurred in 17/255 versus 4/247 participants. The adjusted odds ratio of 4.59 is not a risk ratio, and the estimate is imprecise. CTA collateral selection still requires the trial’s clinical and time-window qualifications.

thrombectomy.name: ANGEL-REBOOT
thrombectomy.question: After failed recanalization or high-grade residual stenosis, does bailout angioplasty/stenting help?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=348, 36 Chinese centres. eTICI 0-2a or residual stenosis >70% after thrombectomy. Tirofiban used off-label in 96%.
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS shift at 90d: common OR 0.86 (95% CI 0.59-1.24, p=0.41). sICH 5% vs 1%. Parenchymal hematoma type 2 3% vs 0. Arterial dissection 14% vs 3%.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Bailout angioplasty/stenting did not help and caused substantially more dissection and hemorrhage.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: The trial tested bailout angioplasty/stenting for defined unsuccessful reperfusion or risk of reocclusion, not simply any failed pass. Dissection occurred in 14% versus 3%. The results do not settle every rescue technique or clinical scenario.

thrombectomy.name: PROTECT-MT
thrombectomy.question: Do balloon guide catheters improve thrombectomy outcomes?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=329, 28 Chinese centres. Balloon guide vs conventional guide catheter. TERMINATED EARLY for safety.
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS at 90d WORSE with balloon guide: adjusted common OR 0.66 (95% CI 0.45-0.98, p=0.037). Mortality 24% vs 16%. No significant difference in ICH.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Balloon guide catheters produced worse functional outcomes; the trial was halted.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: A plausible mechanism for balloon-guide use did not translate into benefit in this trial. Early stopping can overestimate treatment effects; interpret the result with its design, uncertainty and need for replication.

thrombectomy.name: RACECAT
thrombectomy.question: In NONURBAN areas, should suspected LVO bypass the local stroke centre for a thrombectomy centre?
thrombectomy.design: Cluster-randomized, n=1401, nonurban Catalonia. Direct to thrombectomy centre vs nearest stroke centre. Halted for futility.
thrombectomy.outcomes: In the ischemic-stroke population, 90-day ordinal mRS adjusted common OR 1.03 (95% CI 0.82-1.29). Direct transport reduced IV thrombolysis (47.5% versus 60.4%) and increased thrombectomy (48.8% versus 39.4%). Mortality was 27.3% versus 27.2%, without a significant difference.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Direct transport did not significantly improve the primary functional outcome in this network. The trial does not establish that reduced thrombolysis and increased thrombectomy causally cancelled each other out.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: This pragmatic network-specific comparison depends on transport times and service organization. Replication and local system characteristics matter before generalizing beyond Catalonia.

thrombectomy.name: TENSION
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT benefit established large infarct (ASPECTS 3-5) up to 12h, selected mostly by plain CT?
thrombectomy.design: Open-label RCT, n=253, 40 European hospitals + 1 Canadian site. EVT + medical vs medical alone ≤12h from onset. Stopped early for efficacy at the first interim analysis.
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS shift at 90d: adjusted common OR 2.58 (95% CI 1.60-4.15, p=0.0001). Mortality LOWER: HR 0.67 (95% CI 0.46-0.98, p=0.038). sICH 6% vs 5%.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: EVT improves function and survival in ASPECTS 3-5 out to 12h — the European confirmation of the large-core trials.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: Selection used non-contrast CT as the predominant imaging modality — no perfusion study required. With SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT and RESCUE-Japan LIMIT it rounds out the large-core evidence; the ATLAS IPD meta-analysis (Lancet 2026, PMID 42107392) pooled all six large-core trials and found consistent benefit with reduced 90-day mortality (aRR 0.82, 95% CI 0.70-0.97).

thrombectomy.name: LASTE
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT improve outcomes in selected large-core anterior-circulation stroke, including ASPECTS 0-2 in patients younger than 80?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=333: EVT plus medical care versus medical care alone, within 6.5 hours or through the protocol’s unknown-onset negative-FLAIR pathway. ASPECTS ≤5; participants aged ≥80 required ASPECTS 4-5. Stopped early after other positive large-core trials.
thrombectomy.outcomes: Median 90d mRS 4 vs 6; generalized OR 1.63 (95% CI 1.29-2.06, P<0.001). Mortality 36.1% vs 55.5% (adjusted RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.50-0.84). sICH 9.6% vs 5.7%.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: EVT improved outcomes and markedly reduced mortality even with no lower ASPECTS bound.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: LASTE included ASPECTS 0-2 below age 80, but was not the only trial to include very low ASPECTS: ANGEL-ASPECT allowed 0-2 with core 70-100 mL and TESLA allowed 2-5. Mortality benefit was also reported in TENSION. Keep each trial’s eligibility and endpoints distinct.

thrombectomy.name: TESLA
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT benefit large infarct (ASPECTS 2-5) selected by NON-CONTRAST CT alone within 24h?
thrombectomy.design: Bayesian-adaptive RCT, n=300, 47 US centres. NCCT-only ASPECTS 2-5, anterior LVO, EVT vs usual care up to 24h.
thrombectomy.outcomes: Mean utility-weighted mRS: 2.93 vs 2.27; adjusted difference 0.63 (95% CrI -0.09 to 1.34); posterior probability of superiority 0.96 — below the prespecified 0.975 threshold, so the primary end point was NOT met. Mortality 35.3% vs 33.3%; sICH 4.0% vs 1.3%.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Formally neutral, with a favourable trend that just missed its Bayesian success threshold.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: A posterior probability of 0.96 against a bar of 0.975 is a near miss, not a refutation — the credible interval spans both no effect and a clinically relevant benefit. The ATLAS IPD meta-analysis pooling TESLA with the five other large-core trials supports benefit across ASPECTS strata.

thrombectomy.name: DISTAL
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT benefit isolated MEDIUM/DISTAL vessel occlusion (MeVO)?
thrombectomy.design: RCT: 553 enrolled, 543 analyzed after consent withdrawals. Non-dominant/co-dominant M2, M3/M4, A1-A3 or P1-P3 occlusion within 24 hours; salvageable tissue was required at 6-24 hours. Median NIHSS 6; 65% received IV thrombolysis.
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS shift at 90d: common OR 0.90 (95% CI 0.67-1.22, P=0.50) — neutral. Mortality 15.5% vs 14.0%; sICH 5.9% vs 2.6%. 12-month follow-up (Lancet Neurol 2026;25:571-80, PMID 42105785) also neutral: adjusted common OR 0.81 (95% CI 0.59-1.12, p=0.20).
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Routine EVT for mild-to-moderate MeVO stroke is not supported — at 90 days or at 12 months.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: DISTAL and ESCAPE-MeVO (2025) found no benefit of routine EVT for MeVO, and the 2026 AHA/ASA AIS guideline rates EVT for nondominant/codominant M2, distal MCA, ACA or PCA occlusion Class III (no benefit). ORIENTAL-MeVO (NEJM 2026; NIHSS ≥6, median 10), published after that guideline, showed more functional independence with EVT (58.6% vs 46.6%, aRR 1.24) but more sICH (4.7% vs 2.2%); the 2026 SVIN focused guideline now allows EVT to be considered (Class IIb) for codominant/nondominant M2 occlusion with disabling deficit and NIHSS ≥6. Selection by deficit severity remains the open question.

thrombectomy.name: ESCAPE-MeVO
thrombectomy.question: Does EVT benefit medium-vessel occlusion within 12h?
thrombectomy.design: RCT, n=530, 5 countries. MeVO (84.7% MCA-branch) with favourable baseline non-invasive imaging; EVT + usual care vs usual care alone.
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS 0-1 at 90d: 41.6% vs 43.1% (adjusted RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.79-1.15, P=0.61). 90-day mortality HIGHER with EVT: 13.3% vs 8.4% (adjusted HR 1.82, 95% CI 1.06-3.12). sICH 5.4% vs 2.2%.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Neutral primary outcome with a mortality and sICH signal against EVT.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: About 43% of controls reached mRS 0-1. This may help explain a limited margin for added benefit, but that mechanism was not tested. The trial’s mortality and hemorrhage findings must be considered alongside its neutral efficacy result, without assuming all MeVO strokes have a good prognosis.

thrombectomy.name: ANGEL-TNK
thrombectomy.question: Does INTRA-ARTERIAL TNK after successful EVT improve outcomes in late-window LVO?
thrombectomy.design: Open-label blinded-endpoint RCT, n=256, 19 Chinese centres. Anterior LVO 4.5-24h from LKW achieving eTICI 2b-3 after EVT; IA TNK 0.125 mg/kg vs standard medical treatment.
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS 0-1 at 90d: 40.5% vs 26.4% (RR 1.44, 95% CI 1.06-1.95, P=.02). None of the 7 secondary efficacy end points was significant. sICH 5.6% vs 6.2%; 90-day mortality 21.4% vs 21.7%.
thrombectomy.bottomLine: The primary endpoint favored treatment, but no secondary endpoint did. No significant difference in symptomatic ICH or mortality was detected; wide confidence intervals do not establish safety equivalence. Confirmatory trials are needed.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: "Successful" reperfusion (eTICI ≥2b) can still leave distal microvascular territory unperfused — the rationale for chasing it with an IA lytic. Contrast with CHOICE-2 (IA alteplase), also positive on the primary but with a mortality excess. The 2026 AHA/ASA AIS guideline now rates adjunctive IA thrombolytics (urokinase, alteplase or tenecteplase) after mTICI ≥2b reperfusion as Class 2b (may be reasonable); agent, dose and patient selection remain unsettled.

thrombectomy.name: CHOICE-2
thrombectomy.question: Does adjunctive INTRA-ARTERIAL alteplase after successful EVT improve outcomes?
thrombectomy.design: Open-label blinded-endpoint RCT, n=440 randomized (433 analyzed), 14 Spanish centres. LVO treated ≤24h achieving eTICI 2b50-3; IA alteplase 0.225 mg/kg (max 20 mg) over 15 min vs thrombectomy alone.
thrombectomy.outcomes: mRS 0-1 at 90d: 57.5% vs 42.5% (adjusted risk difference 15.0%, 95% CI 5.7-24.3, P=.002). Residual hypoperfusion on follow-up CTP: 28.6% vs 50.5%. BUT 90-day mortality 12.1% vs 6.4% (adjusted difference 5.9%, 95% CI 0.5-11.3, P=.03). sICH 1.4% vs 0.5% (P=.33).
thrombectomy.bottomLine: Positive for excellent outcome with a mortality excess the authors flag as warranting further study — not practice-changing yet.
thrombectomy.teachingPoint: More patients achieved mRS 0-1, while mortality was also higher. The nonsignificant symptomatic-ICH comparison does not establish the cause of the mortality difference. The benefit-risk interpretation remains uncertain and requires the complete evidence, not the primary endpoint alone.

postEVTbp.name: ENCHANTED2-MT
postEVTbp.question: Does intensive SBP lowering to <120 mmHg versus a target of 140-180 mmHg improve outcomes after successful EVT?
postEVTbp.design: RCT, n=821, intensive (<120) vs less-intensive (140-180) SBP control for 72h post successful EVT
postEVTbp.outcomes: Primary (mRS shift at 90d): worse in intensive (common OR 1.37 for poor outcome). Early neurologic deterioration more common.
postEVTbp.bottomLine: Intensive SBP lowering (<120) post-EVT is HARMFUL. Standard target SBP <180.
postEVTbp.teachingPoint: The tested intensive lowering strategy caused harm. This does not establish a universal SBP floor or an indication to raise spontaneous SBP below 140. The 2026 AHA/ASA recommendation against active targeting below 140 after successful anterior-circulation EVT has specific population and time-window limits.

postEVTbp.name: OPTIMAL-BP
postEVTbp.question: Does intensive SBP <140 improve outcomes post-EVT vs SBP <180?
postEVTbp.design: RCT, n=306, Korea: SBP target <140 versus 140-180 mmHg for 24 hours after successful EVT.
postEVTbp.outcomes: mRS 0-2 at 90 days: 39.4% versus 54.4%, worse with intensive lowering. The trial stopped early because of data-safety-monitoring concerns.
postEVTbp.bottomLine: In this selected successfully reperfused population, intensive lowering reduced functional independence at 90 days.
postEVTbp.teachingPoint: Participants had mTICI ≥2b reperfusion and persistent SBP ≥140 mmHg. The 24-hour target <140 performed worse than 140–180. This does not establish a universal 140-mmHg floor: the conventional arm did not use vasopressors solely to raise spontaneous SBP below 140. Newer HOPE evidence evaluates a different selected strategy; individualize interpretation by population and reperfusion.

postEVTbp.name: BP-TARGET
postEVTbp.question: Does SBP 100-129 improve outcomes post-EVT vs SBP 130-185?
postEVTbp.design: RCT, n=324, France, intensive vs standard post-successful EVT
postEVTbp.outcomes: Primary (radiographic intraparenchymal haemorrhage at 24-36h): 42% vs 43% (aOR 0.96, 95% CI 0.60-1.51). Hypotensive events 8% vs 3% (not significantly different); 1-week mortality 7% vs 4%.
postEVTbp.bottomLine: Intensive lowering did not significantly reduce the primary radiographic hemorrhage endpoint. Numerical safety differences do not establish functional harm or safety equivalence.
postEVTbp.teachingPoint: ENCHANTED2/MT (<120) and OPTIMAL-BP (<140) showed worse outcomes with intensive lowering vs a 140-180 target; BP-TARGET (100-129) was neutral and BEST-II (<140/<160) did not meet futility criteria but gave a low predicted probability of benefit. Together they support avoiding intensive SBP lowering after successful EVT, with an upper limit of 180.

postEVTbp.name: BEST-II
postEVTbp.question: Are lower SBP targets (<140 or <160) futile compared with ≤180 mm Hg for 24 h after successful EVT?
postEVTbp.outcomes: Lower SBP targets did NOT meet the prespecified futility criteria (infarct-volume slope -0.29, futility p=0.99; uw-mRS slope -0.0019, futility p=0.93). However, predicted probability of success in a future larger trial was only 25% (<140) and 14% (<160), and uw-mRS was numerically worse with lower targets (0.51 and 0.47 vs 0.58).
postEVTbp.bottomLine: Phase 2 futility trial (n=120): lower targets (<140, <160) did not meet prespecified futility or harm criteria, but a larger trial was predicted to have only a 25% (<140) or 14% (<160) chance of success, so benefit is unlikely (consistent with, not proof of, no benefit).
postEVTbp.teachingPoint: BEST-II is not a harm trial: targets were held for 24 h, lower targets did not meet prespecified futility or harm criteria, and the <140 arm had the smallest mean infarct volume. The harm signal behind the Class III: Harm advice against SBP <140 for the first 72 h after successful EVT comes from ENCHANTED2/MT (<120 for 72 h) and OPTIMAL-BP (<140 for 24 h).

ichReversal.name: INTERACT2
ichReversal.question: Does intensive BP lowering (SBP <140) improve outcomes in acute ICH?
ichReversal.design: RCT, n=2839, intensive (SBP <140 within 1h) vs standard (<180)
ichReversal.outcomes: Primary (mRS 3-6 at 90d): no significant difference. Ordinal analysis favored intensive.
ichReversal.bottomLine: In selected acute mild-to-moderate spontaneous ICH, intensive BP lowering did not significantly improve the binary primary endpoint; the ordinal analysis favored treatment. These findings do not establish safety in severe or large ICH or surgical-decompression candidates.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: AHA/ASA 2022: for mild-to-moderate spontaneous ICH presenting with SBP 150-220 mmHg, targeting 140 and maintaining 130-150 may be reasonable. Safety and efficacy in large/severe ICH or patients requiring decompression are uncertain.

ichReversal.name: ATACH-2
ichReversal.question: Does aggressive BP lowering (SBP 110-139) improve outcomes vs standard (140-179)?
ichReversal.design: RCT, n=1000, aggressive vs standard with nicardipine
ichReversal.outcomes: Primary outcome: no difference. Renal adverse events: 9% vs 4% (higher in aggressive).
ichReversal.bottomLine: The trial compared SBP targets 110-139 and 140-179 mmHg and found no functional benefit, with more renal adverse events in the intensive group.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: AHA/ASA 2022 advises against acute lowering below 130 mmHg in mild-to-moderate spontaneous ICH presenting with SBP >150. This qualified guideline threshold was not a separately randomized 130-mmHg boundary in ATACH-2.

ichReversal.name: INTERACT3
ichReversal.question: Does a care bundle (early intensive BP, glucose, temp, AC reversal) improve ICH outcomes?
ichReversal.design: Cluster RCT, n=7036, bundle vs usual care
ichReversal.outcomes: Ordinal shift mRS at 6mo favored bundle (OR 0.86). Mortality: trend toward benefit.
ichReversal.bottomLine: A bundle of early intensive BP + glucose + fever + AC reversal improves ICH outcomes.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: INTERACT3 tested a care bundle. The randomized comparison establishes the package-level result, not the independent effect of each component or proof that the components reinforce one another.

ichReversal.name: MISTIE III
ichReversal.question: Does minimally-invasive clot lysis (alteplase through catheter) improve ICH outcomes?
ichReversal.design: RCT, n=506, MIS+alteplase vs medical management for supratentorial ICH ≥30 mL
ichReversal.outcomes: The primary mRS 0-3 comparison at 1 year was neutral. An exploratory as-treated analysis associated achieved residual clot ≤15 mL with an adjusted 10.5-percentage-point higher favorable-outcome rate (95% CI 1.0-20.0; P=.03), without multiplicity adjustment; this was not a randomized subgroup effect.
ichReversal.bottomLine: Technical success (clot reduction to <15 mL) correlates with outcome; overall neutral trial.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: MISTIE III and ENRICH studied different minimally invasive approaches and selection criteria. Compare their designs and outcomes without inferring that one trial established the other’s historical origin or that achieved clot reduction is a randomized treatment selector.

ichReversal.name: ENRICH
ichReversal.question: Does minimally-invasive parafascicular surgery (BrainPath) improve lobar ICH outcomes?
ichReversal.design: RCT, n=300, MIPS+medical vs medical for lobar or anterior basal ganglia ICH 30-80 mL within 24h (basal ganglia enrolment stopped after 175 patients by an adaptation rule)
ichReversal.outcomes: Primary (utility-weighted mRS at 180d): significantly favored MIPS.
ichReversal.bottomLine: Minimally invasive parafascicular surgery improved the primary outcome in the selected lobar-ICH subgroup; the overall result was driven by that subgroup.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: Original trial eligibility included age 18-80, ICH 30-80 mL and GCS 5-14; the registry excluded NIHSS <5. Anterior basal ganglia ICH accounted for 30.7% before adaptive restriction to lobar enrollment. Utility-weighted mRS difference: lobar 0.127 (95% CrI 0.035-0.219), anterior basal ganglia -0.013 (-0.147 to 0.116). This is a trial summary, not the separate institutional surgical-screen algorithm; operative timing and all exclusions remain essential.

ichReversal.name: ANNEXA-4 / ANNEXA-I
ichReversal.question: Does andexanet alfa reduce hematoma expansion in factor Xa inhibitor-associated ICH?
ichReversal.design: Single-arm (ANNEXA-4) → RCT (ANNEXA-I): andexanet vs usual care
ichReversal.outcomes: ANNEXA-I: hemostatic efficacy 67% vs 53%. Thrombotic events: 10.3% vs 5.6%, including ischemic stroke 6.5% vs 1.5%.
ichReversal.bottomLine: ANNEXA-I improved hemostatic efficacy but increased thrombosis, without demonstrated 30-day functional or mortality benefit. Andexanet is no longer sold in the US.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: FDA concluded that risks outweigh benefits; AstraZeneca submitted a voluntary BLA-withdrawal request and ended US sales on 22 December 2025. A submitted request is not evidence here of completed regulatory withdrawal. The September 2026 NCS/SCCM update conditionally suggests 4F-PCC over andexanet for spontaneous factor Xa inhibitor-associated ICH (moderate certainty); its traumatic-ICH recommendation has very-low certainty. This comparison does not establish aPCC equivalence.

ichReversal.name: INTERACT4
ichReversal.question: Should BP be lowered in the ambulance, before stroke type is known?
ichReversal.design: RCT, n=2404, China: suspected stroke with motor deficit and SBP ≥150, randomized in an ambulance within 2 hours. SBP target 130-140 versus usual care. Of 2240 imaging-confirmed strokes, 1041 (46.5%) were hemorrhagic.
ichReversal.outcomes: Overall NEUTRAL: common OR 1.00 (95% CI 0.87-1.15). Hemorrhagic subgroup BENEFIT: cOR 0.75 (95% CI 0.60-0.92). Ischemic subgroup HARM: cOR 1.30 (95% CI 1.06-1.60).
ichReversal.bottomLine: The trial does not support routine intensive prehospital lowering to 130-140 mmHg in undifferentiated suspected stroke. Other urgent BP indications require their own assessment.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: Subtype analyses favored treatment in hemorrhagic stroke and suggested harm in ischemic stroke. The hemorrhagic proportion was 46.5% of imaging-confirmed strokes; transportability to a different case mix is uncertain, not a proven change in net treatment effect.

ichReversal.name: TICH-2
ichReversal.question: Does tranexamic acid improve outcome after spontaneous ICH?
ichReversal.design: RCT, n=2325, 124 sites in 12 countries. TXA 1g bolus + 1g over 8h vs placebo within 8h of onset.
ichReversal.outcomes: mRS shift at 90d: aOR 0.88 (95% CI 0.76-1.03, p=0.11). Death by day 7 LOWER: 9% vs 11% (aOR 0.73, p=0.041). 90-day case fatality unchanged: 22% vs 21%. Fewer serious adverse events with TXA.
ichReversal.bottomLine: Tranexamic acid reduced early deaths and serious adverse events but did not significantly improve the primary 90-day functional outcome. This does not establish universal safety or routine benefit in ICH.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: Tranexamic acid reduced early hematoma expansion without a significant primary functional benefit. Earlier treatment or imaging enrichment are hypotheses for future study, not established explanations of the neutral result or proven ways to obtain benefit.

ichReversal.name: CLEAR III
ichReversal.question: Does intraventricular alteplase via EVD improve outcome in IVH?
ichReversal.design: RCT, n=500: stable nontraumatic ICH <30 mL with IVH obstructing the third or fourth ventricle and an EVD in place, without underlying structural pathology. Alteplase 1 mg every 8 hours for up to 12 doses versus saline under the study CT and clinical monitoring protocol.
ichReversal.outcomes: mRS ≤3 at 180d: 48% vs 45% (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.88-1.28, p=0.554). Case fatality LOWER: 18% vs 29% (HR 0.60, p=0.006). But mRS 5 HIGHER: 17% vs 9% (RR 1.99, p=0.007). Ventriculitis 7% vs 12%.
ichReversal.bottomLine: Mortality was lower and mRS 5 more frequent in the alteplase group, while the primary functional endpoint was neutral. Group distributions cannot identify which individual deaths were prevented or predict an individual functional ceiling.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: Discuss the group-level survival and severe-dependence outcomes with the patient’s values. The trial does not prove that a particular patient will survive with a fixed disability level.

ichReversal.name: STICH / STICH II
ichReversal.question: Does early open surgical evacuation improve outcome in supratentorial ICH?
ichReversal.design: STICH: n=1033 in 27 countries, surgery within 24 hours after randomization versus initial conservative care. STICH II: n=601, superficial lobar ICH 10-100 mL without IVH, surgery within 12 hours after randomization. Initial conservative care permitted rescue surgery.
ichReversal.outcomes: STICH: favourable outcome 26% vs 24% (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.66-1.19, p=0.414). STICH II: unfavourable 59% vs 62% (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.62-1.20, p=0.367).
ichReversal.bottomLine: Neither trial found benefit from routine early craniotomy — the basis for medical management as default.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: Neither trial demonstrated a significant primary functional benefit; STICH II remained compatible with a small survival advantage. These supratentorial trials do not apply to cerebellar ICH with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus requiring surgical assessment.

ichReversal.name: RESTART
ichReversal.question: Is it safe to restart antiplatelet therapy after intracerebral hemorrhage?
ichReversal.design: RCT, n=537, 122 UK hospitals. Patients on antithrombotics when ICH occurred, randomized a median of 76 days later to start vs avoid antiplatelet therapy.
ichReversal.outcomes: Recurrent ICH: 4% (12/268) vs 9% (23/268), adjusted HR 0.51 (95% CI 0.25-1.03, p=0.060). Major hemorrhagic events 7% vs 9%. Major occlusive events 15% vs 14%.
ichReversal.bottomLine: No statistically significant increase in recurrent ICH was detected in the selected population; the estimate favored antiplatelet restart but remained imprecise.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: The results are reassuring for selected patients with an antiplatelet indication after ICH, but timing-specific uncertainty remains. Randomization included 21 patients at 1-6 days and 118 at 7-30 days. Extended follow-up recurrent-ICH HR was 0.87 (95% CI 0.49-1.55), so the trial does not guarantee no increased risk for every patient or restart time.

ichReversal.name: SWITCH
ichReversal.question: Does decompressive craniectomy (WITHOUT clot evacuation) help severe DEEP supratentorial ICH?
ichReversal.design: Open-label assessor-blinded RCT, n=197 analyzed, 42 European stroke centres. Basal ganglia or thalamic ICH (median volume 57 mL), age 18-75; craniectomy + best medical treatment vs best medical treatment alone. Stopped early for lack of funding.
ichReversal.outcomes: mRS 5-6 at 180d: 44% vs 58% (adjusted RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.59-1.01, adjusted risk difference -13%, p=0.057).
ichReversal.bottomLine: Weak evidence that craniectomy might reduce death-or-worst-disability in severe deep ICH — hypothesis-supporting, not definitive.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: This is decompression WITHOUT evacuation — do not conflate with ENRICH (lobar, evacuation). p=0.057 in an early-stopped trial, and survival in both arms was frequently with severe disability — so frame any craniectomy discussion around what outcome the patient would accept, not survival alone.

ichReversal.name: FASTEST
ichReversal.question: Does rFVIIa given within 2h of ICH onset improve functional outcome?
ichReversal.design: Double-blind placebo-controlled adaptive phase 3 RCT, n=626, 93 sites in 6 countries. Spontaneous ICH 2-60 mL, GCS ≥8, no recent anticoagulation; rFVIIa 80 μg/kg IV vs placebo, mean onset-to-drug 100 min. Stopped for futility at the second interim analysis.
ichReversal.outcomes: Primary (mRS 0-2/3/4-6 at 180d): adjusted common OR 1.09 (95% CI 0.79-1.51, p=0.61) — NEGATIVE. Hematoma growth reduced at 24h: ICH -3.7 mL, ICH+IVH -5.2 mL. Life-threatening thromboembolic events ≤4d: <5% vs 1% (RR 3.41, 95% CI 1.14-10.15, p=0.020).
ichReversal.bottomLine: Even at a mean 100 minutes from onset, hemostatic therapy slowed bleeding but did not improve function — and increased life-threatening thrombotic events.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: Despite less hematoma growth, the futility-stopped trial did not show a functional benefit. Routine rFVIIa or tranexamic acid for non-anticoagulant-associated spontaneous ICH remains distinct from indicated reversal of an anticoagulant; further enrichment research does not establish current benefit.

ichReversal.name: TRIDENT
ichReversal.question: Does adding a single low-dose triple-combination BP pill after ICH prevent recurrent stroke?
ichReversal.design: Double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, n=1670. ICH survivors with SBP 130-160 mmHg on standard care; triple pill (telmisartan 20 mg / amlodipine 2.5 mg / indapamide 1.25 mg) vs placebo after a 2-week active run-in. Median follow-up 2.5y.
ichReversal.outcomes: Recurrent stroke: 4.6% vs 7.4% (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.41-0.92, P=0.02). Mean SBP during follow-up 127 vs 138 mmHg. Major CV events 6.6% vs 9.8% (P=0.04).
ichReversal.bottomLine: Intensified BP lowering with a low-dose triple pill cut recurrent stroke by roughly 40% after ICH.
ichReversal.teachingPoint: The tested treatment strategy reduced recurrent stroke, with achieved mean SBP 127 versus 138 mmHg. An achieved group mean is not a universal target. A creatinine rise of at least 20% was the most common reason for discontinuation, supporting careful renal monitoring.

secondaryPrevention.name: CHANCE
secondaryPrevention.question: Does DAPT (clopidogrel + ASA) reduce stroke after minor stroke/TIA?
secondaryPrevention.design: RCT, n=5170, Chinese, clopi+ASA x 21d vs ASA alone
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: Short-course DAPT reduces early recurrence after minor stroke/high-risk TIA.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: Inclusion: NIHSS ≤3 or ABCD² ≥4. DAPT duration 21 days (longer duration increases bleeding).

secondaryPrevention.name: POINT
secondaryPrevention.question: Does DAPT reduce stroke in minor stroke/TIA (US/international)?
secondaryPrevention.design: RCT, n=4881, clopi+ASA planned x90d; halted early for lower ischemic events but higher major hemorrhage
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: 90-day major ischemic events: 5.0% vs 6.5%, HR 0.75. Major bleeding: 0.9% vs 0.4%.
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: DAPT reduces ischemic events but increases bleeding. Optimal duration appears to be about 21 days (POINT time-course analysis, Johnston et al., Circulation 2019; pooled CHANCE-POINT patient-level analysis, Pan et al., JAMA Neurol 2019).
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: The evidence supports early short-course DAPT in eligible acute noncardioembolic minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA (ABCD² ≥4), after excluding hemorrhage and assessing reperfusion and anticoagulation indications. POINT tested 90 days; the 21-day emphasis comes from subsequent time-course and pooled analyses.

secondaryPrevention.name: THALES
secondaryPrevention.question: Does ticagrelor + ASA reduce stroke/death in minor-to-moderate AIS or high-risk TIA?
secondaryPrevention.design: RCT, n=11,016, ticagrelor+ASA x 30d vs ASA alone
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: 30-day stroke or death: 5.5% vs 6.6%, HR 0.83. Severe bleeding: 0.5% vs 0.1%.
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: Ticagrelor+ASA effective in up to NIHSS 5 or high-risk TIA with atherosclerosis.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: THALES included noncardioembolic stroke with NIHSS ≤5 and selected high-risk TIA. Genotype-directed ticagrelor evidence comes separately from CHANCE-2 in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers with minor stroke or high-risk TIA; do not extend that evidence automatically to all THALES-eligible patients.

secondaryPrevention.name: CHANCE-2
secondaryPrevention.question: In CYP2C19 LOF carriers, is ticagrelor+ASA better than clopidogrel+ASA?
secondaryPrevention.design: RCT, n=6412, ticagrelor+ASA vs clopi+ASA x 21d in CYP2C19 LOF carriers
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: Among the selected Chinese CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers with acute minor stroke or high-risk TIA, ticagrelor modestly reduced stroke compared with clopidogrel but increased total bleeding. This is not an automatic switch rule for every carrier.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: CYP2C19 loss-of-function can impair clopidogrel activation. The trial addresses treatment in selected carriers; it does not establish one population-wide carrier prevalence or current local access to point-of-care testing.

secondaryPrevention.name: SPARCL
secondaryPrevention.question: Does atorvastatin 80 mg reduce recurrent stroke in non-cardioembolic stroke/TIA?
secondaryPrevention.design: RCT, n=4731: atorvastatin 80 mg daily versus placebo after recent stroke or TIA.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: Small increase in hemorrhagic stroke (2.3% vs 1.4%) but overall net benefit. Informed later TST trial showing LDL <70 target.

secondaryPrevention.name: TST (Treat Stroke to Target)
secondaryPrevention.question: Is LDL <70 better than 90-110 for secondary stroke prevention?
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: TST supports an LDL-C goal below 70 mg/dL after ischemic stroke or TIA with atherosclerotic disease; current goals are risk-stratified.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: For stroke/TIA with atherosclerotic disease, the 2021 AHA/ASA guideline recommends statin therapy, with ezetimibe if needed, toward LDL-C <70 mg/dL and selected PCSK9 escalation. The 2026 dyslipidemia guideline uses LDL-C <55 mg/dL for very-high-risk ASCVD; apply its full risk definition.

secondaryPrevention.name: ARCADIA
secondaryPrevention.question: Does apixaban reduce recurrent stroke in ESUS patients with atrial cardiopathy markers?
secondaryPrevention.design: RCT, n=1015: apixaban versus aspirin after cryptogenic stroke without documented AF, with atrial cardiopathy defined by P-wave terminal force in V1 >5000 µV·ms, NT-proBNP >250 pg/mL, or indexed left-atrial diameter ≥3 cm/m².
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: Primary: no significant difference. Recurrent stroke: 4.4% vs 4.4% per year (40 events in each arm; HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.64-1.55).
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: Empiric anticoagulation in ESUS with atrial cardiopathy markers does NOT reduce recurrence.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: Apixaban did not reduce recurrent stroke in this atrial-cardiopathy population without AF. Individualized extended rhythm monitoring is a separate guideline-supported diagnostic strategy; the trial did not compare anticoagulation with mandatory loop-recorder implantation.

secondaryPrevention.name: NAVIGATE-ESUS + RE-SPECT ESUS
secondaryPrevention.question: Does rivaroxaban or dabigatran reduce recurrence in ESUS?
secondaryPrevention.design: Two large RCTs of DOAC vs ASA in ESUS
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: Both neutral for efficacy. NAVIGATE-ESUS: major bleeding 1.8% vs 0.7%/y (HR 2.72). RE-SPECT ESUS: major bleeding not significantly higher (HR 1.19, 95% CI 0.85-1.66) but more clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding.
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: Empiric AC in ESUS does not help. Find the etiology.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: ESUS includes heterogeneous mechanisms. These trials do not support routine empiric anticoagulation without an established indication; they do not negate anticoagulation benefit when AF or another specific indication is subsequently found.

secondaryPrevention.name: CLOSE / RESPECT / REDUCE
secondaryPrevention.question: Does PFO closure reduce recurrent stroke in patients with cryptogenic stroke + PFO?
secondaryPrevention.design: Three RCTs, closure vs medical management
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: All favored closure, particularly in patients with large shunt or atrial septal aneurysm.
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: PFO closure recommended in select cryptogenic stroke patients age <60 with high-risk PFO features.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: PASCAL combines RoPE with large shunt or atrial septal aneurysm to assess PFO attribution. ESO 2024 recommends closure plus antiplatelet therapy in selected 18-60-year-olds with PFO-associated stroke and generally suggests against closure when attribution is unlikely, unless clinical causality is high. AHA/ASA 2021 rates closure in the selected high-risk-PFO population as reasonable (Class IIa). Use shared assessment.

secondaryPrevention.name: CADISS / TREAT-CAD
secondaryPrevention.citation: CADISS Lancet Neurol 2015;14:361-7 (PMID 25684164); TREAT-CAD Lancet Neurol 2021;20:341-50 (PMID 33765420)
secondaryPrevention.question: Antiplatelet vs anticoagulation for cervical artery dissection?
secondaryPrevention.design: CADISS compared clinician-selected antiplatelet regimens with anticoagulation for 3 months. TREAT-CAD compared aspirin 300 mg daily with a vitamin K antagonist for 90 days. These randomized regimens are distinct from later individualized treatment-duration recommendations.
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: CADISS: no significant difference in stroke/death but underpowered (event rates lower than expected). TREAT-CAD: aspirin did NOT meet non-inferiority vs VKA — more composite endpoint events with ASA (23% vs 15%), driven mainly by clinical ischaemic strokes (7 [8%] on aspirin vs 0 on VKA); subclinical MRI outcomes were similar between arms (15% vs 13%).
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: Antiplatelet and anticoagulation are both reasonable for cervical artery dissection (2021 AHA/ASA secondary-prevention guideline, Class 2a); TREAT-CAD did not confirm aspirin non-inferiority, so the choice is individualized.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: Treatment choice requires individualized assessment of ischemic and bleeding risks. TREAT-CAD did not establish aspirin noninferiority. These trials do not validate occlusion, pseudoaneurysm or free-floating thrombus as independent treatment-effect selectors.

secondaryPrevention.name: CREST
secondaryPrevention.question: Carotid endarterectomy versus carotid artery stenting for carotid stenosis
secondaryPrevention.design: RCT, n=2502, CEA vs CAS in symptomatic and asymptomatic carotid stenosis
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: Similar 4-year primary composite. Peri-procedural stroke higher with CAS; peri-procedural myocardial infarction higher with CEA. Age interaction: CAS favoured in younger patients, CEA in older.
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: CEA and CAS give similar overall outcomes; the peri-procedural risk profile differs by procedure and by age.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: The trade-off is the teaching point: stenting front-loads stroke risk, endarterectomy front-loads cardiac risk, and a stroke and an MI are not equivalent to a patient. For what modern medical therapy alone achieves in ASYMPTOMATIC disease, see the separate CREST-2 card — it found adding stenting reduced 4-year events, so do not read CREST as licensing medical management alone.

secondaryPrevention.name: CONVINCE / CHANCE-3
secondaryPrevention.question: Does anti-inflammatory therapy with colchicine prevent recurrent stroke?
secondaryPrevention.design: CONVINCE: open-label RCT, n=3144, colchicine 0.5mg daily long-term vs usual care. CHANCE-3: double-blind RCT, n=8343, colchicine × 90 days vs placebo, hs-CRP ≥2 mg/L required.
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: CONVINCE: 9.8% vs 11.7% (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.68-1.05, p=0.12); CRP fell at all timepoints. CHANCE-3: new stroke at 90d 6.3% vs 6.5% (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.83-1.16, p=0.79).
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: Both neutral — colchicine is not established for stroke prevention.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: CHANCE-3 did not demonstrate reduced 90-day stroke with its colchicine regimen in a CRP-enriched population. CONVINCE stopped early because of COVID-related funding limitations and remained compatible with a longer-term benefit. Neither result settles every anti-inflammatory drug, duration or population.

secondaryPrevention.name: CREST-2
secondaryPrevention.question: In ASYMPTOMATIC ≥70% carotid stenosis, does adding revascularization to intensive medical therapy help?
secondaryPrevention.design: Two parallel observer-blinded RCTs, 155 centres in 5 countries. Stenting trial n=1245; endarterectomy trial n=1240. Each compared intensive medical management alone vs medical management + revascularization.
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: 4-year stroke/death ≤44d or later ipsilateral stroke — Stenting: 2.8% (95% CI 1.5-4.3) vs 6.0% (95% CI 3.8-8.3), p=0.02. Endarterectomy: 3.7% (95% CI 2.1-5.5) vs 5.3% (95% CI 3.3-7.4), p=0.24.
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: Adding stenting reduced 4-year events; adding endarterectomy did not reach significance.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: The two parallel trials did not randomize stenting against endarterectomy, so differing results do not demonstrate stenting superiority over surgery. Medical-only primary-event rates were about 5-6% at 4 years; comparisons with 1990s trials require matched populations, endpoints and follow-up.

secondaryPrevention.name: ECST-2
secondaryPrevention.question: For carotid stenosis with LOW-to-INTERMEDIATE predicted stroke risk, is medical therapy alone enough?
secondaryPrevention.design: RCT, n=429 (2-year interim), 30 centres in Europe/Canada. Stenosis ≥50% with 5-year predicted ipsilateral stroke risk <20% by Carotid Artery Risk (CAR) score. OMT alone vs OMT + revascularization. Hierarchical win-ratio endpoint.
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: No benefit from added revascularization at 2 years on the hierarchical composite (periprocedural death/fatal stroke/fatal MI → non-fatal stroke → non-fatal MI → new silent infarct).
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: In risk-stratified low-to-intermediate-risk stenosis, optimised medical therapy alone held up at 2 years.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: ECST-2 required both ≥50% stenosis and a CAR-predicted 5-year ipsilateral stroke risk <20%. It included asymptomatic and selected symptomatic disease. Its 2-year interim result does not establish CAR as a sole treatment rule; longer follow-up remains important.

secondaryPrevention.name: ESPRIT (BP) / BPROAD
secondaryPrevention.question: Is an SBP target <120 better than <140 in patients with diabetes or prior stroke?
secondaryPrevention.design: ESPRIT n=11,255 (3022 with prior stroke, 4359 with diabetes), median 3.4y. BPROAD n=12,821 with type 2 diabetes, median 4.2y. Both open-label, blinded outcomes, China.
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: ESPRIT: 9.7% vs 11.1% (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.78-0.99, p=0.028), no heterogeneity by diabetes or prior stroke. BPROAD: 1.65 vs 2.09 per 100 person-years (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69-0.90, p<0.001).
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: The tested SBP target below 120 reduced composite vascular events in selected high-risk populations. ESPRIT included prior-stroke participants; this is not a universal target for every stroke survivor.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: ESPRIT found no detected treatment-effect heterogeneity by prior stroke or diabetes, but this does not prove equal benefit in every subgroup. These were chronic prevention strategies in selected participants, not acute-stroke targets. Balance benefit against syncope in ESPRIT and symptomatic hypotension and hyperkalemia in BPROAD, using the complete current guideline and patient context.

secondaryPrevention.name: SAVE
secondaryPrevention.question: Does CPAP reduce CV events in moderate-severe OSA?
secondaryPrevention.design: RCT, n=2717, CPAP vs usual care in established CV disease with OSA
secondaryPrevention.outcomes: Primary composite CV endpoint: no significant difference.
secondaryPrevention.bottomLine: SAVE did not demonstrate fewer cardiovascular events with CPAP at the observed mean adherence of 3.3 hours per night in mostly minimally sleepy participants with established cardiovascular disease.
secondaryPrevention.teachingPoint: Treating OSA can improve sleepiness and sleep-related quality of life and may improve BP. OSA is associated with poorer stroke outcomes, but association does not establish causation. SAVE leaves uncertainty about vascular benefit in other populations or with different adherence.

antithrombotic.name: RE-LY / ROCKET-AF / ARISTOTLE / ENGAGE AF
antithrombotic.question: Are DOACs non-inferior or superior to warfarin for AF stroke prevention?
antithrombotic.outcomes: All DOACs non-inferior or superior. Less ICH across all DOACs.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: DOACs are first-line over warfarin for non-valvular AF.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: ARISTOTLE found lower mortality and major bleeding with apixaban than warfarin. Its dose reduction to 2.5 mg twice daily required at least two of: age ≥80 years, weight ≤60 kg, or serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL. Apply the complete current product labeling, including renal and interaction requirements.

antithrombotic.name: ELAN
antithrombotic.question: When to start DOAC after AF-related ischemic stroke — early vs late?
antithrombotic.design: RCT, n=2013. Imaging-defined minor/moderate infarcts: early DOAC within 48 hours; major infarcts: day 6-7. Later treatment: day 3-4 for minor, day 6-7 for moderate and day 12-14 for major infarcts.
antithrombotic.outcomes: At 30 days, recurrent ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, major extracranial bleeding, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage or vascular death occurred in 2.9% early versus 4.1% later (risk difference -1.18 percentage points, 95% CI -2.84 to +0.47). ELAN estimated this difference without formal superiority or noninferiority testing. Symptomatic ICH occurred in 0.2% in each arm.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: Early DOAC initiation by ELAN imaging severity showed no excess ICH versus later start and supports earlier treatment in selected AF-stroke patients.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: ELAN classified stroke severity by imaging-defined infarct size/territory, not NIHSS cutoffs. NIHSS-based buckets can be a bedside heuristic, but should not be presented as ELAN criteria. CATALYST IPDMA (Dehbi et al., Lancet 2025, n=5441 pooling ELAN/OPTIMAS/TIMING/START) broadly supports early initiation without excess sICH.

antithrombotic.name: OPTIMAS
antithrombotic.question: Is early DOAC initiation after AF stroke non-inferior to standard timing?
antithrombotic.design: Pragmatic open-label RCT in UK, n>3500, early (≤4 days) vs standard (7-14 days)
antithrombotic.outcomes: At 90 days, recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, unclassifiable stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 3.3% in each group. Early treatment met the prespecified 2-percentage-point noninferiority margin; observed safety outcomes were similar.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: DOAC initiation within 4 days was noninferior to initiation at 7-14 days within the prespecified margin in eligible participants. Noninferiority is not proof of identical efficacy or unrestricted safety.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: OPTIMAS tested ≤4 days versus 7-14 days; ELAN used imaging-stratified schedules and a different estimation design. These trials inform earlier treatment decisions but do not measure how most centers currently practice.

antithrombotic.name: CAPRIE
antithrombotic.question: Is clopidogrel superior to aspirin for secondary prevention of vascular events?
antithrombotic.design: RCT, n=19,185, clopidogrel 75 mg vs ASA 325 mg
antithrombotic.outcomes: Annual rate of the composite of ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction or vascular death: 5.32% with clopidogrel versus 5.83% with aspirin; relative risk reduction 8.7% in the overall trial population.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: Clopidogrel provided a modest overall composite-event reduction versus aspirin. This overall estimate should not be presented as a separately established stroke-entry-subgroup effect.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: Clopidogrel and ASA are both acceptable first-line single antiplatelets for non-cardioembolic stroke. Patient factors (cost, GI bleeding history, concurrent PPI) often drive the choice.

antithrombotic.name: MATCH
antithrombotic.question: Does long-term clopidogrel+ASA reduce stroke recurrence vs clopidogrel alone?
antithrombotic.outcomes: Primary composite vascular events: no significant difference. Life-threatening bleeding: 2.6% vs 1.3%, NNH=78.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: Long-term DAPT after stroke is NOT effective and increases bleeding.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: Along with CHARISMA and CHANCE/POINT time-course analyses, supports short-course DAPT (~21 days) rather than prolonged dual therapy in most minor stroke/TIA patients.

antithrombotic.name: SPS3
antithrombotic.question: Does DAPT (clopi+ASA) reduce recurrent lacunar stroke?
antithrombotic.design: RCT, n=3020, clopi+ASA vs ASA alone, mean 3.4 years
antithrombotic.outcomes: Recurrent stroke: HR 0.92, NS. Major hemorrhage: HR 1.97. Mortality: HR 1.52 (increased with DAPT).
antithrombotic.bottomLine: DAPT does NOT reduce lacunar stroke recurrence; increases bleeding and mortality.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: Critical: long-term DAPT does not reduce lacunar stroke recurrence and increases bleeding and death — use single antiplatelet therapy long-term. Short-course DAPT is for minor stroke/high-risk TIA; cardioembolic stroke from AF needs oral anticoagulation, not antiplatelets.

antithrombotic.name: COMPASS
antithrombotic.question: Does rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BID + ASA reduce MACE in stable atherosclerotic disease?
antithrombotic.design: RCT, n=27,395, stable CAD or PAD
antithrombotic.outcomes: MACE: HR 0.76 (24% RRR). Stroke: HR 0.58. Major bleeding: HR 1.70 (no ICH increase).
antithrombotic.bottomLine: Low-dose rivaroxaban + ASA reduces stroke/CV events in polyvascular disease.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: The regimen was studied in selected stable CAD/PAD, with increased major bleeding. Prior hemorrhagic or lacunar stroke, stroke within 1 month, and a need for anticoagulation were exclusions. Polyvascular disease may identify greater absolute risk, but the trial is not a general anticoagulation strategy for stroke survivors.

antithrombotic.name: LAAOS III
antithrombotic.question: Does surgical LAA occlusion during cardiac surgery prevent stroke?
antithrombotic.design: RCT, n=4770: AF with CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 (mean 4.2), already undergoing cardiac surgery. LAA occlusion versus no occlusion with usual care, including intended anticoagulation; 76.8% were receiving oral anticoagulation at 3 years. Mean follow-up 3.8 years.
antithrombotic.outcomes: Stroke or systemic embolism 4.8% vs 7.0% (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.53-0.85, p=0.001). 76.8% still anticoagulated at 3 years. No difference in perioperative bleeding, heart failure or death.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: Concomitant surgical occlusion cut stroke by a third — ADDITIVE to anticoagulation, not a replacement.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: The design detail that changes everything: three-quarters remained on anticoagulation. LAAOS III supports occlusion in patients already having cardiac surgery. It says nothing about percutaneous LAAO as an anticoagulation substitute — that is OPTION’s question.

antithrombotic.name: OPTION
antithrombotic.question: After AF ablation, can LAA closure REPLACE oral anticoagulation?
antithrombotic.design: RCT, n=1600, CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 (men) / ≥3 (women), post-ablation. Percutaneous LAA closure vs oral anticoagulation, 36 months.
antithrombotic.outcomes: Non-procedural major/CRNM bleeding 8.5% vs 18.1% (p<0.001 superiority). Death/stroke/systemic embolism 5.3% vs 5.8% (p<0.001 non-inferiority). Device/procedure complications in 23 patients.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: After AF ablation, LAA closure was noninferior within the prespecified 5-percentage-point margin for the efficacy composite, with less nonprocedural major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: OPTION evaluated replacement of long-term anticoagulation after an initial postimplant regimen of anticoagulation plus aspirin for 90 days, followed by aspirin. This differs from LAAOS III, which added surgical occlusion to usual care; do not extrapolate OPTION beyond its postablation population.

antithrombotic.name: NOAH-AFNET 6
antithrombotic.question: Should device-detected atrial high-rate episodes be anticoagulated?
antithrombotic.design: Double-blind RCT, n=2536, age ≥65 with AHRE ≥6 min (median 2.8h) and ≥1 stroke risk factor, NO ECG-documented AF. Edoxaban vs placebo. Stopped early.
antithrombotic.outcomes: CV death/stroke/systemic embolism 3.2%/y vs 4.0%/y (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.60-1.08, p=0.15). Stroke ~1%/y in BOTH arms. Death or major bleeding INCREASED: 5.9%/y vs 4.5%/y (HR 1.31, p=0.03). 18.2% progressed to ECG-confirmed AF.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: Anticoagulating device-detected AHRE did not reduce events and increased death or major bleeding.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: Stroke incidence was about 1% per year in both arms, with uncertainty around benefit and increased safety events with edoxaban. Read alongside ARTESiA, which found a modest stroke reduction with apixaban and more major bleeding. Device-detected episodes require individualized benefit-risk assessment, not an automatic treatment rule.

antithrombotic.name: LOOP
antithrombotic.question: Does implantable loop recorder screening for AF prevent stroke?
antithrombotic.design: RCT, n=6004, age 70-90 with ≥1 stroke risk factor, randomized 1:3 to ILR vs usual care. Anticoagulation recommended for AF ≥6 min. Median follow-up 64.5 months.
antithrombotic.outcomes: AF detected 31.8% vs 12.2% (HR 3.17, p<0.0001). Anticoagulation started 29.7% vs 13.1% (HR 2.72, p<0.0001). Stroke or systemic embolism 4.5% vs 5.6% (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.61-1.05, p=0.11). Major bleeding 4.3% vs 3.5%.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: Tripling AF detection and doubling anticoagulation did not significantly reduce stroke.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: The authors put it best: not all AF is worth screening for, and not all screen-detected AF merits anticoagulation. A powerful lesson that a surrogate (detection) is not an outcome (stroke prevented).

antithrombotic.name: INVICTUS
antithrombotic.question: Can a DOAC replace warfarin in rheumatic heart disease with AF?
antithrombotic.design: RCT, n=4531, AF with echocardiographic rheumatic heart disease. Mean age 50.5, 72.3% women. Rivaroxaban vs dose-adjusted VKA.
antithrombotic.outcomes: Restricted mean survival free of the primary composite (stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction or vascular/unknown-cause death) was 1675 days with VKA versus 1599 with rivaroxaban; difference -76 days (95% CI -121 to -31). The separate all-cause survival difference was -72 days. No significant major-bleeding difference was detected.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: VKA is preferred for AF with rheumatic mitral stenosis or moderate-or-greater mitral stenosis. The result should not exclude DOACs solely because another form of valve disease is present.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: Rivaroxaban was inferior to VKA in the enrolled rheumatic-heart-disease AF population. A nonsignificant major-bleeding comparison does not by itself explain the excess mortality or establish its mechanism.

antithrombotic.name: OCEANIC-AF
antithrombotic.question: Can the factor XIa inhibitor asundexian replace apixaban in AF?
antithrombotic.design: Double-blind RCT, n=14,810, high-risk AF (mean CHA2DS2-VASc 4.3). Asundexian 50mg daily vs standard-dose apixaban. STOPPED EARLY.
antithrombotic.outcomes: Stroke or systemic embolism 1.3% vs 0.4% — asundexian nearly FOUR-FOLD worse (HR 3.79, 95% CI 2.46-5.83). Major bleeding LOWER with asundexian: 0.2% vs 0.7% (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.18-0.55).
antithrombotic.bottomLine: Asundexian is inferior to apixaban for AF despite causing less bleeding.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: The essential counterweight to OCEANIC-STROKE, where asundexian ADDED to antiplatelets helped non-cardioembolic stroke. Add-on to antiplatelet therapy is not the same as substitution for a DOAC. Less bleeding is worthless if thrombosis quadruples.

antithrombotic.name: CASSISS
antithrombotic.question: With better selection and experienced operators, does intracranial stenting beat medical therapy?
antithrombotic.design: RCT: 380 randomized, 358 confirmed eligible, at 8 Chinese centers. Symptomatic 70-99% intracranial stenosis with TIA or nondisabling nonperforator-territory stroke; enrolled more than 3 weeks after the latest event. Stenting plus medical therapy versus medical therapy alone; 3-year follow-up.
antithrombotic.outcomes: No significant difference in stroke/death at 30 days or qualifying-territory stroke through 1 year; no difference at 2 or 3 years; no mortality difference.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: Stenting did not demonstrate added benefit in this selected population; the primary HR was 1.10 (95% CI 0.52-2.35), so the result does not prove zero effect.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: The trial used experienced operators, excluded qualifying perforator-territory stroke, and delayed enrollment beyond 3 weeks. The findings do not support routine added stenting under these conditions, while leaving uncertainty about other specifically selected rescue scenarios.

antithrombotic.name: CMOSS
antithrombotic.question: Does EC-IC bypass help symptomatic ICA/MCA occlusion when patients are selected by perfusion imaging?
antithrombotic.design: RCT, n=324, 13 Chinese centres. ICA or MCA occlusion with hemodynamic insufficiency on CT perfusion. Bypass + medical vs medical alone. Median age 52.7.
antithrombotic.outcomes: Stroke/death ≤30d or ipsilateral stroke to 2 years: 8.6% (13/151) vs 12.3% (19/155); incidence difference -3.6% (95% CI -10.1% to 2.9%) — not significant.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: The modern re-test of the 1985 EC-IC Bypass Study reached the same conclusion.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: With the tested perfusion selection and contemporary surgical approach, bypass did not significantly improve the primary outcome. This result does not establish a universal rule about whether future trials may use better patient selection or a new mechanism.

antithrombotic.name: BASIS
antithrombotic.question: Does planned submaximal balloon angioplasty, with rescue stenting permitted, plus aggressive medical therapy improve outcomes versus medical therapy alone for symptomatic ICAS?
antithrombotic.design: Open-label blinded-endpoint RCT, n=501, 31 Chinese centres. 70-99% intracranial stenosis with TIA <90d or stroke 14-90d before enrolment; submaximal angioplasty + aggressive medical management vs medical management alone.
antithrombotic.outcomes: Primary composite (stroke/death ≤30d, or ischemic stroke in the territory / revascularization of the qualifying artery through 12mo): 4.4% vs 13.5% (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.16-0.63, P<.001). 30-day stroke/death 3.2% vs 1.6%. Procedural complications 17.4%; arterial dissection 14.5%.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: First positive endovascular ICAS trial — fewer late events, bought with real upfront procedural risk.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: BASIS used planned submaximal angioplasty after the specified interval from stroke, with rescue stenting allowed; 71.4% of patients with dissection received rescue stents. Later symptom-driven revascularization contributed to the primary composite, but a post hoc composite excluding it also favored intervention. Generalizability beyond the studied Chinese population remains uncertain.

antithrombotic.name: CAPTIVA
antithrombotic.citation: Design paper: Hoh et al. Int J Stroke 2025;20:623-8 (PMID 39862061); NCT05047172 — ONGOING, no efficacy results yet
antithrombotic.question: Is ticagrelor + ASA or low-dose rivaroxaban + ASA superior to clopidogrel + ASA for symptomatic 70-99% ICAS?
antithrombotic.design: Original planned design: double-blind three-arm RCT targeting 1683 patients at more than 100 US/Canadian sites, comparing ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily or clopidogrel 75 mg daily, each with aspirin 81 mg and intensive risk-factor management for 12 months after a qualifying ischemic infarct within 30 days. This describes the original plan, not the later arm status.
antithrombotic.outcomes: Status update, February 2026: the NIH/NINDS announcement identified termination of the low-dose rivaroxaban arm for safety and futility. This is a stopping announcement, not a final efficacy result. Remaining study dates and arm status require the current sponsor or registry record.
antithrombotic.bottomLine: Low-dose rivaroxaban is out for ICAS; the ticagrelor-vs-clopidogrel question remains open.
antithrombotic.teachingPoint: Note the contrast with COMPASS, where the same rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BID dose helped stable coronary/peripheral atherosclerosis — intracranial disease keeps punishing anticoagulation-based strategies. Until CAPTIVA reads out, clopidogrel + ASA × 90 days with intensive risk-factor management remains the ICAS default.

rehabilitation.name: AVERT
rehabilitation.question: Does very early (<24h) intensive mobilization improve stroke outcomes?
rehabilitation.design: RCT, n=2104, very early intensive vs usual care
rehabilitation.outcomes: mRS 0-2 at 3 months: 46% versus 50%, less favorable with very early intensive mobilization. A separate observational analysis associated more daily sessions with better outcomes (OR 1.13 per session) but longer daily duration with worse outcomes (OR 0.94 per additional 5 minutes).
rehabilitation.bottomLine: Very-early (<24h) HIGH-intensity mobilization is HARMFUL. Early mobilization is fine but not aggressively intensive in first 24h.
