rehabilitation.teachingPoint: Avoid equating early mobilization with the tested intensive regimen. The dose-response analysis was observational across both arms and did not establish an optimal or universally safe session schedule.

rehabilitation.name: FOCUS
rehabilitation.question: Does fluoxetine improve motor recovery after stroke?
rehabilitation.design: RCT, n=3127, fluoxetine 20 mg vs placebo x 6 months
rehabilitation.outcomes: Modified Rankin at 6 mo: no significant difference. Fewer depression cases but more fractures with fluoxetine.
rehabilitation.bottomLine: Fluoxetine did not improve the primary functional outcome and should not be used routinely solely to promote stroke recovery.
rehabilitation.teachingPoint: FOCUS, AFFINITY and EFFECTS tested functional outcomes, rather than the identical direct-motor endpoint used in FLAME. Their results do not support routine fluoxetine for recovery. Treatment of diagnosed depression is a separate indication requiring its own assessment.

rehabilitation.name: AFFINITY
rehabilitation.question: Does fluoxetine improve functional recovery in an ethnically diverse population (Australia, New Zealand, Vietnam)?
rehabilitation.design: RCT, n=1280, fluoxetine vs placebo x 6 months
rehabilitation.outcomes: Functional outcome (mRS shift): no significant difference (adjusted common OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.76-1.15, p=0.53). Excess falls (3% vs 1%), bone fractures (3% vs 1%), and epileptic seizures (2% vs <1%).
rehabilitation.bottomLine: Fluoxetine did not improve the primary functional outcome, consistent with FOCUS; the trial does not support routine use solely for stroke recovery.
rehabilitation.teachingPoint: Do not prescribe fluoxetine solely in expectation of improved functional recovery from these results. Management of diagnosed post-stroke depression, including drug choice, is a separate clinical question.

rehabilitation.name: VNS-REHAB
rehabilitation.question: Does vagus nerve stimulation paired with rehabilitation improve chronic arm weakness after stroke?
rehabilitation.design: Triple-blind, sham-controlled device RCT, n=108, at 19 UK/US services. Adults aged 22-80, 9 months to 10 years after ischemic stroke, with FMA-UE 20-50. All received an implant; active VNS versus 0 mA stimulation paired with 18 in-clinic sessions over 6 weeks, then home exercise.
rehabilitation.outcomes: Change in Fugl-Meyer Upper Extremity the day after in-clinic therapy favoured paired VNS; FMA-UE response rate at 90 days also higher.
rehabilitation.bottomLine: Paired VNS improved upper-limb impairment versus sham in selected chronic ischemic-stroke patients. FDA granted premarket approval for the device in August 2021 (PMA P210007).
rehabilitation.teachingPoint: An implanted sham comparator helps isolate the stimulation effect from surgery. Randomization, rather than an assumed plateau in every participant, supports the between-group inference. The primary endpoint was impairment (FMA-UE); activity/function and quality-of-life measures were also collected.

neurocriticalCare.name: INTREPID
neurocriticalCare.question: Does preventing fever after acute vascular brain injury improve outcome?
neurocriticalCare.design: Open-label RCT with blinded outcomes, n=677 (254 ischemic, 223 ICH, 200 SAH), 43 ICUs in 7 countries. Automated surface cooling to 37.0°C for 14 days vs standard tiered treatment at ≥38°C.
neurocriticalCare.outcomes: Fever burden markedly reduced — prevention is achievable. But 3-month mRS shift was FUTILE at planned interim analysis; enrolment stopped at 686 of a planned 1176.
neurocriticalCare.bottomLine: Fever can be prevented; preventing it did not improve function.
neurocriticalCare.teachingPoint: INTREPID compared preventive temperature control with reactive fever treatment; both groups received fever care. It cannot establish whether any fever treatment is beneficial or prove that fever is merely a noncausal marker of injury severity.

neurocriticalCare.name: SETPOINT2
neurocriticalCare.question: Does early tracheostomy improve outcomes in ventilated severe stroke?
neurocriticalCare.design: RCT, n=382, 26 US and German neurocritical care centres. Early tracheostomy ≤5 days (done in 95.2%, median day 4) vs standard weaning with tracheostomy from day 10 if needed (done in 67%, median day 11). 6-month outcome.
neurocriticalCare.outcomes: No significant difference in the proportion without severe disability (mRS 0-4 vs 5-6) at 6 months.
neurocriticalCare.bottomLine: Early tracheostomy did not improve 6-month outcome.
neurocriticalCare.teachingPoint: In the standard group, 43/194 (22%) were successfully extubated and 21/194 (10.8%) died before tracheostomy. Thus, the roughly one third without the procedure were not all avoidable operations. The mRS 0-4 versus 5-6 endpoint reflects the study’s patient-preference framework, not a universal functional ceiling.

neurocriticalCare.name: CHARM
neurocriticalCare.question: Can IV glibenclamide prevent malignant cerebral edema after large hemispheric infarction?
neurocriticalCare.design: Phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, 143 centres in 21 countries. ASPECTS 1-5 or core 80-300 mL, drug started within 10h. Primary analysis in ages 18-70. Enrolled 535; STOPPED EARLY by sponsor for COVID-related slow enrolment, before unblinding.
neurocriticalCare.outcomes: Primary (ages 18-70, n=431): 90-day mRS shift common OR 1.17 (95% CI 0.80-1.71, p=0.42) — no significant benefit; underpowered after early termination. 90-day mortality 32% vs 29% (glibenclamide vs placebo; HR 1.20, p=0.30); hypoglycaemia 6% vs 2% (safety population).
neurocriticalCare.bottomLine: Pharmacologic prevention of malignant edema remains unproven.
neurocriticalCare.teachingPoint: Halted for operational, not scientific, reasons — so this is an underpowered trial, not a demonstrated absence of effect. An important distinction when reading "negative" trials. Decompressive hemicraniectomy remains the intervention with proven mortality benefit.

sahCvt.name: ISAT
sahCvt.question: Coiling vs clipping for ruptured aneurysms?
sahCvt.bottomLine: Coiling reduced death or dependency at 1 year in selected ruptured aneurysms judged suitable for either procedure. This is not a universal advantage for most aneurysms or every time horizon.
sahCvt.teachingPoint: Treatment choice depends on aneurysm anatomy, patient characteristics and multidisciplinary assessment. AHA/ASA 2023 favors coiling for 1-year function in selected good-grade anterior-circulation aSAH equally suitable for both approaches; both can provide favorable long-term outcomes.

sahCvt.name: Nimodipine (BANT + meta-analyses)
sahCvt.question: Does nimodipine improve outcomes in aSAH?
sahCvt.design: BANT (British Aneurysm Nimodipine Trial, 1989, n=554) + Cochrane meta-analyses
sahCvt.outcomes: Poor outcome (death or dependency): oral nimodipine RR 0.67 (95% CI 0.55-0.81) in the Cochrane review; BANT: cerebral infarction 22% vs 33%, poor outcome 20% vs 33%. No definite effect on angiographic vasospasm.
sahCvt.bottomLine: Oral nimodipine 60 mg q4h × 21 days is Class 1 standard of care for all aSAH.
sahCvt.teachingPoint: Nimodipine improves aSAH outcomes, but its precise protective mechanism is not established. AHA/ASA 2023 supports continued dosing when hypotension can be managed; significant BP variability may require temporary interruption. A split-dose regimen is not a universal instruction established by BANT.

sahCvt.name: SAHIT
sahCvt.question: Prognostic model for aSAH outcomes
sahCvt.outcomes: Prediction of 3-month Glasgow Outcome Scale: the core model uses age, premorbid hypertension and neurological grade; the imaging model adds clot volume, aneurysm size and location; the full model also adds treatment modality.
sahCvt.bottomLine: Externally validated score for outcome prediction.
sahCvt.teachingPoint: Use with caution — communicates prognosis probabilistically, not deterministically. Patients occasionally do dramatically better or worse than predicted.

sahCvt.name: ISAT (18-year)
sahCvt.question: Does the early advantage of coiling over clipping persist long term?
sahCvt.design: Long-term follow-up of the UK ISAT cohort, n=1644, randomized 1994-2002, followed 10.0-18.5 years.
sahCvt.outcomes: Alive at 10y: 83% (coiling) vs 79% (clipping), OR 1.35 (95% CI 1.06-1.73). Alive AND independent: OR 1.34 (95% CI 1.07-1.67). Independent among responders 82% vs 78%. 33 late recurrent SAH, 17 from the target aneurysm.
sahCvt.bottomLine: In the long-term UK follow-up, favorable functional outcome was assessed at 10 years, while survival and rebleeding surveillance extended up to 18 years. These are different endpoints and follow-up horizons.
sahCvt.teachingPoint: Answers the durability objection to coiling. The higher rebleed and re-treatment rate after coiling is real but small in absolute terms, and does not erase the survival benefit. Applies to aneurysms in genuine equipoise — mostly small anterior-circulation lesions in good-grade patients.

sahCvt.name: PHASES
sahCvt.question: What is the 5-year rupture risk of an incidental unruptured aneurysm?
sahCvt.design: Pooled individual-patient analysis of six prospective cohorts, n=8382, 29,166 person-years, 230 ruptures.
sahCvt.outcomes: Mean 1-year rupture risk 1.4% (95% CI 1.1-1.6); 5-year 3.4% (95% CI 2.9-4.0). Predictors: Population, Hypertension, Age, Size, Earlier SAH, Site. 5-year absolute risk ranges 0.25% to >15%. Finnish 3.6× and Japanese 2.8× baseline risk.
sahCvt.bottomLine: PHASES converts an incidental aneurysm into an absolute 5-year rupture risk.
sahCvt.teachingPoint: The 60-fold spread (0.25% to >15%) is what makes treat-versus-observe a real calculation rather than a reflex. Crucially, PHASES gives only the rupture side — you must weigh it against the procedural risk of treatment, which it does not model.

sahCvt.name: SAHaRA
sahCvt.question: Liberal or restrictive transfusion in anemic aSAH patients?
sahCvt.design: RCT, n=742 at 23 centers: mandatory red-cell transfusion at hemoglobin ≤10 g/dL in the liberal group versus optional transfusion at ≤8 g/dL in the restrictive group during critical care.
sahCvt.outcomes: At 12 months, mRS ≥4 occurred in 33.5% versus 37.7% (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.72-1.09; P=.22). FIM 82.8 versus 79.8. EQ-5D-5L showed no significant difference (difference 0.02, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.09); adverse events were similar.
sahCvt.bottomLine: The liberal strategy did not demonstrate a significant functional advantage at 12 months. The confidence interval does not establish equivalence or exclude meaningful benefit.
sahCvt.teachingPoint: A nonsignificant superiority result is not proof of no effect: the interval permits a 28% relative reduction through a 9% relative increase in unfavorable outcome. A transfusion recommendation requires the broader evidence and individual context, not this result alone.

sahCvt.name: ULTRA
sahCvt.question: Does ultra-early tranexamic acid improve outcome in aSAH?
sahCvt.design: RCT, n=955, Netherlands. TXA from diagnosis until aneurysm treatment or 24h vs usual care.
sahCvt.outcomes: mRS 0-3 at 6 months: 60% vs 64% (adjusted OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.66-1.12). Rebleeding before treatment 10% vs 14% (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.48-1.04). Serious adverse events comparable.
sahCvt.bottomLine: No outcome benefit despite a trend toward less rebleeding.
sahCvt.teachingPoint: Reducing an intermediate event (rebleeding) did not translate into function. The practical message is to prioritize prompt aneurysm securing over pharmacologic bridging.

sahCvt.name: EARLYDRAIN
sahCvt.question: Does prophylactic lumbar CSF drainage improve 6-month functional outcome and reduce secondary infarction after aSAH?
sahCvt.design: RCT, n=287, 19 centres in Germany, Switzerland and Canada. Lumbar drain 5 mL/h started within 72h, after aneurysm securing within 48h.
sahCvt.outcomes: Unfavorable outcome (mRS 3-6) at 6 months: 32.6% vs 44.8% (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.52-0.98, p=0.04). Secondary infarction at discharge 28.5% vs 39.9% (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.49-0.99, p=0.04).
sahCvt.bottomLine: One of the few POSITIVE interventions in aSAH critical care.
sahCvt.teachingPoint: The trial reduced secondary infarction and 6-month disability; it did not use the current composite DCI definition. Treatment followed aneurysm securing and excluded compressed/absent basal cisterns and therapeutic anticoagulation. Drainage was postponed for ICP >20 mmHg or a craniospinal gradient >5 mmHg; this summary is not a stand-alone drain-management protocol.

sahCvt.name: TO-ACT
sahCvt.question: Does endovascular treatment help severe cerebral venous thrombosis?
sahCvt.design: Open-label RCT with blinded endpoint, n=67, at 8 hospitals in 3 countries. Severe CVT with altered mental status, coma, ICH or thrombosis of the deep cerebral venous system. EVT plus standard care versus standard care alone; stopped for futility at the first interim analysis.
sahCvt.outcomes: No benefit on mRS 0-1 at 12 months.
sahCvt.bottomLine: This randomized trial of EVT for severe CVT stopped for futility. Its small size and selected population limit inference about individual rescue-treatment scenarios.
sahCvt.teachingPoint: Small (n=67), so it does not exclude benefit in the most catastrophic presentations, but it removes any basis for ROUTINE endovascular therapy. Anticoagulation remains first-line even in severe CVT, which is how the 2024 AHA CVT statement frames it.
